# Shared Keys and Generations

A user owns several devices and wants all of them to read the same data. A
team has many members with the same wish. In both cases there must be a key
that every authorised party holds and no unauthorised party holds, and the
set of authorised parties changes over time: devices are lost, members leave.
This chapter describes the *per-user key* (PUK) and *per-team key* (PTK),
how they are distributed, how they are replaced when membership changes, and
how old data stays readable afterwards. It ends with the application keys
derived from them.

## The problem with a shared key

Give a group one symmetric key and every member can read everything. Remove
a member and the key is no longer secret from an outsider, so it must be
replaced. Replacing it raises two questions. How do the remaining members
receive the new key without the departed member also receiving it? And what
happens to everything that was encrypted under the old key?

The first question is answered by public-key encryption: the new key is
boxed (as in [Chapter 4](04-hybrid-encryption.qmd)) to each remaining
member's public key, and the departed member is simply left off the list.
The second is answered by not re-encrypting old data at all, but by making
the new key able to unlock the old one. Both ideas are old; FOKS's
contribution is a concrete, verifiable data structure for them.

## Terminology: which secrecy is this?

The repository's guide calls the property that follows "forward secrecy via
generational seeds". The term needs care, because in the literature it means
something narrower.

- *Forward secrecy*, in its original sense, is the property that compromise
  of a party's long-term keys does not reveal *past* session keys. It is
  usually achieved with ephemeral keys that are deleted after use.
- *Post-compromise security* (Cohn-Gordon, Cremers and Garratt) is the
  property that after a compromise, the protocol can *heal*: once the
  compromised party is excluded or updates its keys, future messages are
  again secret from the attacker. Unger et al. survey this under the name
  "future secrecy" as well.

FOKS's generational keys give a *removal-time* guarantee: a party that held
generation $g$ and was excluded before generation $g+1$ cannot read anything
encrypted under $g+1$ or later. That is the post-compromise / future-secrecy
family, applied to group membership. It is explicitly *not* forward secrecy
in the ephemeral-key sense: a current member's newest seed unlocks every
earlier generation (that is the point of the seed chain), so compromising
one device today reveals the whole history of what that device was entitled
to read. The book uses the term "forward secrecy" for this property only when
quoting the repository; otherwise it says "post-removal secrecy".

## PUK, PTK, roles and generations

A PUK or PTK is a 32-byte random seed. From it, `derive_key` (see
[Chapter 3](03-key-hierarchy.qmd)) produces an Ed25519 verify key, whose
entity type is 14 (PUK) or 15 (PTK), and an HEPK. So a shared key can both
sign (team certificates, bearer-token challenges) and receive boxes.

There is one seed per *role* and per *generation*. Roles are totally ordered:

| Role | Order | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| None | 0 | no access |
| Member | 1 | carries a signed 16-bit *visibility* level; a member with higher visibility outranks one with lower |
| Admin | 2 | |
| Owner | 3 | |

When a team is created, four PTK seeds are generated, ordered member-min,
member, admin, owner. The seed for role $r$ is boxed to every party whose
role is at least $r$. In the client, the device-side filter is
`receiver.role >= rotation.role` and the team-side filter is
`rotation.role <= receiver.role`; both say the same thing. An owner can open
every role's key, an admin cannot open the owner key, and a reader cannot
open admin material. Data encrypted under the member key is readable by
everyone; data encrypted under the admin key is readable only by admins and
owners.

The *generation* is a counter starting at 1 that increments every time the
seed for a role is replaced.

## Parcels and box sets

When a device wants a shared key it fetches a *parcel* from the server:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `generation`, `role` | which seed the parcel delivers |
| `hybrid` | the hybrid box addressed to this recipient |
| `target`, `target_host`, `target_role`, `target_generation` | the recipient and, for PTKs boxed to a PUK, which PUK generation the box was addressed to |
| `sender` | the entity that sealed the box |
| `box_id` | the 16-byte ID of the box set this box came from |
| `temp_dh_key` | the signed temporary key, if the sender was on a different curve |
| `seed_chain` | boxes for every earlier generation (next section) |

The server assembles the parcel from a stored box set and the accumulated
chain. Note what the server does *not* have: any seed. It stores ciphertext
and routes it.

For a PTK the recipient of each box is a member *user*, not a device: the
team key is boxed to the user's PUK HEPK, and the user's devices reach it by
first opening their own PUK. The code comments that "the receiver entity is
the owning user or team, not its verify key". This indirection means a team
rotation does not need to know about every member's devices, and a user's
device change does not touch any team.

### The plaintext binds its context

What gets encrypted in a shared-key box is not the bare 32-byte seed. It is

```
[[receiver, host], generation, role, seed]
```

canonically encoded. On opening, the recipient compares the decoded
receiver, host, generation and role to what the verified chain says the
parcel should contain, and rejects the seed on any mismatch. A box for one
role cannot be presented as a box for another; a box for one host cannot be
replayed on another. This is the same defence-in-depth idea as the typed
nonce: since XSalsa20-Poly1305 has no associated-data input, the context is
placed inside the authenticated plaintext instead.

Decoding a seed plaintext has a small subtlety. The generic Snowpack decoder
would copy the 32 seed bytes into an ordinary heap vector inside its value
tree, which is neither zeroized nor tracked. `foks-crypto` therefore checks
that the plaintext ends in a 32-byte binary field, copies those bytes into
zeroizing storage, overwrites them with zeros in the buffer, and only then
runs the decoder on the redacted bytes.

## The seed chain

Suppose a rotation replaces generation $g$ with $g+1$. The remaining members
receive $g+1$ in new boxes. But files, directory entries and messages
encrypted under $g$, $g-1$, and so on still exist, and re-encrypting all of
them would be expensive and would still leave the old ciphertexts on the
server.

The rotating party instead encrypts the *previous* seed under a key derived
from the *new* seed:

```
SeedChainBox {
    generation: g,
    role:       r,
    secret_box: XSalsa20-Poly1305(
                    key   = derive_key(seed[g+1], 2),
                    nonce = BE64(SHARED_KEY_SEED_TYPE_ID) ‖ 16 random bytes,
                    msg   = [[party, host], g, r, seed[g]] )
}
```

The server stores every chain box and returns the whole chain with a parcel.
A recipient that has opened the hybrid box for generation $N$ then walks the
chain backwards:

```
  hybrid box            chain box            chain box
  ┌──────────┐   key    ┌──────────┐   key    ┌──────────┐
  │ seed[N]  │ ───────> │ seed[N-1]│ ───────> │ seed[N-2]│ ───> ...  seed[1]
  └──────────┘ derive   └──────────┘ derive   └──────────┘
   (public-key)          (symmetric)           (symmetric)
```

For each box, in reverse order, the recipient requires
`box.generation == newer.generation - 1` and the same role, derives
`derive_key(newer.seed, 2)`, opens the box, checks `[receiver, host,
generation, role]` against expectations, and continues. The result is the
list of all seeds, oldest first. One public-key operation unlocks $N$
generations; the rest is symmetric and cheap. Each hop is authenticated by
Poly1305 under a key only the holder of the newer seed can derive, so the
server cannot splice a foreign seed into the chain, and the strict
generation check means it cannot drop a link either.

Team chains have one variation. The Go implementation creates a single
global chain per rotated PTK, binds the chain's informational receiver
field to the editor who performed the rotation, and attaches the same chain
to every recipient's parcel. `foks-rs` follows this: the team-chain opener
checks host, generation and role but not receiver, and the caller then binds
each recovered seed to the team's public-key history from the verified
chain.

## Rotation

Two events trigger a rotation.

- **Device revocation.** When a user revokes a device, the client generates
  a fresh PUK seed for every role the user holds, boxes each new seed to
  every remaining device of sufficient role, seals a seed-chain box carrying
  the old seed under the new one, and publishes a chain link that names the
  revoked device and the new PUK generations.
- **Member removal or role change.** When an admin removes a team member or
  lowers their role, the same happens for the affected PTK roles, with the
  boxes addressed to the remaining members' PUKs.

The revoked device or removed member holds seeds up to $g$. It never receives
a box for $g+1$, and $g+1$ is fresh randomness with no relation to $g$, so
nothing encrypted under $g+1$ is readable to it. Existing members lose
nothing, because the chain gives them $g$ from $g+1$. This is the whole of
the post-removal secrecy argument.

### Signed by the new keys

A rotation link is signed by more than one key, and the order is fixed. Each
new shared key signs first, in shared-key order, over the link and the
signatures already accumulated; the acting device (or, for a hardware
parent, the P-256 key) signs last. The stacking rule, where every signature
covers the ones before it, is described in
[Chapter 7](07-hardware-keys.qmd). Its purpose here is to prove *possession*
of the new seed at the moment the link is published: a link that announces a
PUK verify key without a signature from the matching seed is rejected. A
server, or a malicious admin who has not actually generated the key, cannot
announce a rotation on someone else's behalf.

## Application keys

Shared seeds are never used directly to encrypt data. Each application gets
its own subtree:

```
app_root = derive_key(seed, 5)
app_key  = typed_hmac(app_root, APP_KEY_DERIVATION_TYPE_ID, encode([0, {"0": app_index}]))
```

with `app_index` 0 for the key-value store and 1 for real-time chat. The
key-value store then derives two more keys from `app_key` under
`KV_KEY_DERIVATION_TYPE_ID`: a MAC key (index 1) for integrity bindings on
directory roots and entries, and a box key (index 2) for encrypting
per-directory and per-file seeds. Real-time chat derives per-purpose keys
(channel name, channel description, message data) under its own type ID.
The repository guide says that "application index 5 derives the kv_app
key"; 5 is the derivation type for the application root, and the key-value
store is application 0 beneath it.

The important structural point is that the PUK/PTK-derived box key encrypts
only *seeds*, never data. A directory has its own seed; a large file has its
own seed; those seeds encrypt the actual bytes. So a rotation re-encrypts a
handful of small seed boxes, not the store. [Chapter 14](14-kv-store.qmd)
and [Chapter 16](16-chat.qmd) follow these keys down to the data.

## Trade-offs

The seed chain deliberately sacrifices forward secrecy among current members
for simplicity and cost. Any member's current seed unlocks the entire
history of their role. A design that wanted forward secrecy as well would
have to delete old seeds and re-encrypt or discard old data, which is at
odds with a store whose purpose is to keep data.

Rotation cost is linear in the number of recipients: one hybrid box (about
1.2 kB) per remaining member per rotated role. For a team of a thousand
members with four roles that is several megabytes per removal. FOKS accepts
this because removals are rare and the server does the storage; the
alternative, tree-based group key agreement as in MLS, would reduce the cost
to logarithmic but at a large increase in protocol complexity and with
different trust assumptions about the server.

Finally, the roles are a lattice with a single chain (None < Member < Admin
< Owner), which keeps the "box to everyone of at least this role" rule
simple. Visibility levels within Member allow finer distinctions without
breaking the order.

## Where to look

- `foks-crypto` (`lib.rs`): `shared_key_seed_plaintext`,
  `seal_puk_seed_chain_box`, `open_shared_key_seed_chain`,
  `open_team_shared_key_seed_chain`, `open_shared_key_parcel_with`,
  `decode_with_redacted_trailing_seed`, `make_software_puk_change_link`,
  `make_yubi_puk_rotation_link`, `derive_kv_keys`, `derive_shared_public`.
- `foks-crypto` (`realtime.rs`): `derive_realtime_keys`.
- `foks-proto` (`role.rs`, `key_material.rs`): `Role`, `RoleType`,
  `SharedKeyBoxSet`, `SharedKeyBox`, `SeedChainBox`, `PukParcel`.
- `foks-client` (`device.rs`, `team/rotation/`): the revocation and
  member-change flows that decide who receives which box.
